skill.displayName: Pet Adaptive Drying Temperature Recommendation | 宠物烘干温度自适应推荐

llm.summary: The skill performs the advertised pet media analysis, but it also silently creates or reuses an identity, logs into a remote service, stores tokens locally, and can retrieve cloud history without clear user-controlled consent.

dimensions.detail: The skill reads workspace environment identity values, may read data/smyx-api-key.txt, uploads local files or URLs to configured lifeemergence.com APIs, and uses a broad shared data directory; these are high-impact data flows for the user-facing purpose.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The package uses Python scripts plus bundled common analysis dependencies and pinned requirements. I did not find install-time persistence, shell execution, scheduled tasks, or remote code retrieval in the inspected artifacts.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The manifest explicitly instructs automatic triggering for pet media and automatic cloud-history lookup, and tells the agent not to ask for or reveal identity values; that under-scopes user control for media upload and account-linked history access.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The common library creates a workspace SQLite database, persists default user records, and stores token/open_token and profile fields; it also silently calls /sys/phoneLogin with register=1 to obtain authorization tokens.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: Remote image/video analysis and report generation fit the stated pet drying recommendation purpose, but automatic identity creation/reuse, cloud history lookup, and token-backed account behavior materially expand the capability beyond a simple one-off pet analysis tool.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable with pet images/videos and report history being processed by the configured lifeemergence.com services, with the skill silently creating or reusing a local identity and storing authorization tokens in a workspace SQLite database. Users should receive clear notice and control over upload, account creation, history lookup, retention, and deletion before this is treated as low risk.
llm.findings:
[TP4] unexpected: The broad filesystem and identity concern is substantiated in part: artifacts show local default identity persistence, reading an API-key/open-id file, silent remote login/registration, and token storage. This supports Review, not a malicious verdict by itself.
[YR4] expected: Manual review did not find offensive tooling or exploit behavior. The match appears tied to manifest/metadata text rather than actionable malicious code.
[SDI-1] unexpected: The analysis wrapper is mostly a generic API client adapted to the pet drying scene code, but the hidden/listing history mode and implicit identity handling are broader than a single media-analysis request.
[SDI-2] unexpected: The local User model includes token, open_token, email, birthday, age, and realname fields, and RequestUtil can save server-returned tokens and user information locally; this is not proportionately disclosed for pet drying recommendations.
[LP3] unexpected: Network calls and file reads are expected for uploaded media analysis, but the skill does not provide a narrow permission boundary for identity files, remote login, token reuse, or cloud history retrieval.
[SQP-1] unexpected: The default trigger on pet media can lead to remote processing or local saving when the user may only have provided an image/video, so explicit intent should be required before upload or history access.
[SQP-2] expected: Saving uploaded media and sending it to server APIs is core to the stated function and is mentioned, but retention, sharing, deletion, and account-linkage are not explained clearly enough.
[SQP-3] expected: Chinese-only CLI status/help text is a usability and disclosure limitation, not evidence of malware.
[P9] expected: Manual inspection of the reported whitespace area found formatting alignment in Python code, not hidden instructions.
